title: A Temple of Paramitas
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of generosity in Buddhist practice, not just as an external act of giving, but also as a way of cultivating inner qualities such as acceptance, understanding, and effort. This generosity is about reconnection and healing, recognizing that giving and receiving are part of a natural flow of energy and non-differentness. By embracing this practice, we can work towards a deeper sense of freedom, kindness, and awakening, even in the face of challenges and imperfections.

So, our tradition teaches that there are six core practices for bodhisattvas.
There are all kinds of lists, but six core practices.
These are the famous paramita practices, practices that go beyond themselves.
These practices help bodhisattvas develop towards Buddhahood, and they are also the main ways that bodhisattvas help other beings.
I think in this universe that we're talking about, we are both the bodhisattvas and the suffering beings, so we have to also help ourselves.
I was thinking these six practices are very much in evidence from the existence of this building that we're sitting in.
This is a paramita project here.
I want to especially focus on four of them, which are so obviously needed in abundance.
We must have been practicing these or this couldn't have happened.
We would have given up long ago, sold the building back, or who knows what, or gotten so mad at each other that we all quit the sangha and everything ground to a halt.
That is possible.
That can happen.
It does happen.
Anyway, here's the list of six, whether they're old friends or you're new to these.
Good friends to meet and remember.
The first is generosity, dana paramita, the Sanskrit.
Second is ethics, sila paramita, shila paramita.
It's [unclear: "like a soft shot"].
The third is patience, shanti paramita.
Fourth is energy, birya paramita.
The fifth is concentration, jhana paramita.
And the sixth is wisdom, prajna paramita.
There's a ton to explore about these.
There are several fairly recent, last five years, really good books on them by two great teachers in our lineage and a really great Buddhist studies scholar.
There are many other books besides.
It's a very well-known topic, and there's so much to it.
Each one of these you could study for a lifetime.

So I just want to take a quick brush through them, especially, like I said, the four, and reflect a little about their presence and their activity and their challenges as we've built and completed this building.
Remodeled, I guess.
It was such a big remodel it feels like we built it.
Number one is pretty easy to relate to: generosity.
Oh, my goodness.
It's like a vibrating field of generosity, being here.
An astounding flood of generosity, right?
Our generous donors, the almost unbelievable number of volunteer hours.
Good thing we didn't try to add them up.
We would have blown our minds.
People have put those hours into this going way back, at least to the campaign committee when we started our capital campaign in 2021, and continuing through this very afternoon.
People were in here painting.
This brown line made it from there all the way to there right before you got here.
By Friday, Saturday, it'll probably connect.
Maybe Saturday evening, when we'll have a big opening ceremony, we'll take all the tape off really quick and sweep, sweep, sweep before people arrive, and say, welcome, it's all done.
So how generous is that?
People setting aside big chunks of their lives, devoting themselves to being here.
Whether you made it to a work party, which is amazing, or just being here tonight, which is amazing, or you've done hundreds, thousands of hours, oh, my goodness.

And not just us, but the generosity of many professionals and officials who, although yes, it was their job, have almost to a person, maybe everybody involved that we interacted with, been so generous.
I was talking to our really kind and generous contractor this afternoon.
He's gotten to be friends with the main building inspector who was assigned to this project, and he talked a lot about how generous that guy was.
Jonathan is his name.
He talked about how much Jonathan worked with our contractor to facilitate getting through the final approvals, which, after feeling totally stuck in the mud, were suddenly all done.
That was a week and a half ago, the day before we were last here.
So there's been a lot of generosity here.

This practice is called generosity, but each of these practices invites some depth beyond, deeper and more complete, with maybe some layers we don't usually think about when we use these words in everyday speech.
So regular generosity is certainly here, certainly true: giving gifts, gifts of time, gifts of money, gifts of kindness.

But the paramita part, dana paramita, generosity beyond generosity or deep generosity, is also looking at the underlying situation, the underlying universe into which generosity is happening, and re-understanding what's going on there.
In conventional generosity, we tend to think: I'm over here.
In this particular case, I have more resources, time, money, expertise, than this person over there who looks like she's in need.
So I help her.
Here is the gift I'm giving.
There's a separateness there, right?
I'm here, you're there.
That often works just fine, no biggie, until it doesn't.
Every one of us has had the experience of trying to give something to somebody and they didn't like it.
How could that be?
Somehow it seemed condescending or overbearing or it wasn't the thing they wanted.
Did we even ask?
So there's something to that separateness that puts the brakes on the real possibilities of generosity.
So dana paramita, Buddhist generosity, is this: as I practice giving, can I use it as a practice of going beyond this sense of separation, this sense of me over here, you over there?
Actually it's just the flowing of natural generosity, universe giving.
Receiving and giving are no different.
Giving and receiving is just this amazing flow of energy and non-differentness, non-separateness.
Sometimes we use the word emptiness, which is a little confusing-sounding: the giver and the gift and the receiver are empty of any separate anything.
And there's a trauma, right?
There's a trauma from separation.
It's our root trauma.
Life is a journey to try to reconnect, right?
So these practices are also practices of reconnection and healing.
There's a lot to it, if you think about it.
So So generosity is an expression of that interconnectedness, that interbeing.
That also makes it much more natural, right?
I don't have to decide, I guess I'll give you that.
Of course, we already have it together.
The classic example here is your left hand gets a splinter, and your right hand isn't like, eh, I guess I'll give you the tweezers, I don't know.
You should really have your own pair of tweezers.
Were you paying attention?
You're clumsy.
No, you just take it out, right?
They're more like two hands in one body than separate people.
That is the paramita, the going beyond part.
That's so evidently here.
I think we had, of course, a mix of conventional generosity, sometimes with a little stickiness.
It happens, right?
We're human.
And we had tremendous vast amounts of this deep dana paramita, this generosity beyond generosity, just giving freely out of love and joy.
And the sense here, too, of a bigger purpose.
I think that helped us a lot, actually.
If we had just thought we were doing this for our meditation club, I think we wouldn't have gotten anywhere.
We had some sense of something much bigger than just the people in this room, or the full room last week.
It's not just for us, right?
It's for the greater community.
It's for the people that come after us.
I was thinking about that.
That's part of the generosity of this: 100 years from now, we hope, someone will be wandering around in Bellingham and say, look at that, it's the [unclear: "Un-Buddha Center"].
I think I'll go there.
They won't have any idea of us.
We'll be long gone.
Maybe at the 50th or the 100th anniversary they'll tell old stories, or produce a little book.
Maybe you'll end up a little picture in the book.
But eventually that book will be lost.
They won't know us, but we gave them that, right?
We gave a huge gift to people that we can't ever meet.
So that's dana paramita.
Isn't that beautiful?
We hope.
The second practice, I think so clearly here, no question about this one, is patience practice, right?
Kshanti paramita.
And here, just like with dana, with generosity, the everyday meaning of patience is perfectly apt.
It took time.
We just passed the third anniversary of purchasing the building.
Did you know that?
And finally we're in here.
Of course everybody says it takes longer than you think, and you're like, yeah, yeah, yeah, I know.
And then it really takes longer than you think.
Oh, my gosh.
So we really had to be persistent and patient.
Our contractor is a pretty good estimator, actually.
But his estimate, well, he didn't know that we were doing so much, I think, at first.
His original estimate was a six-month construction cycle, and he started in November, so we should have been done at the end of May according to that.
And here it is the end of August.
So, yes, it takes time.
I've been kind of public about how impatient I got last month and the month before.
I was like, okay, I'm going to probably go practice in the building now.
And all the leaders were like, Tim, no permit, hello.
We can wait a little longer.
Remember your practice.
No, get in there.
I had all kinds of good reasons.
But now we're here.
So there's conventional patience.
Sometimes conventional patience is a little limited, right?
It has this quality of, again, separation.
I'm over here putting up with this nonsense until it's the way I want it, and then I'm done with patience.
Good, I was patient.
This deeper patience is more about looking deeply at what's going on here.
What is this feeling that we call impatience?
Where is it coming from?
What are its causes?
How am I creating it, so we stop just externalizing it all?
It's the building department's fault or something like that.
Deep patience points to the most fundamental point in all of Buddhism, right?
We can't get away from this point, nor should we.
The Buddha expressed it as the Four Noble Truths: the minute you want something to be other than it is, you're going to suffer.
It's pretty simple.

And yet we forget that and get annoyed at somebody else or something else, or argue for something and maybe take a little sidestep around our values to get what we want sooner, whether that's cutting in line or breaking occupancy laws or whatever.
So deep patience is really taking us right back to that.
Right back to who is the one who wants, who is the one who's desiring or averse to something, who is the one who's not really accepting things as they are.

The deep patience is freedom: to deeply understand that, to work with it directly, to breathe with it, to feel that little knot in your stomach or your shoulders or wherever it hangs out that doesn't want it to be this way, or doesn't want that other person to be the way that you think they are.
Of course it gets complicated fast because we're humans.
And mistakes are made, right?
I don't know how many decisions we made creating this building.
Hundreds?
North of a thousand, probably?
Not all those were the best decision, no question, right?
We had a system of who made those decisions which more or less worked most of the time, and a loose agreement about when this group consults with that group or the whole sangha.
Some things we did a lot of process around, and some things were like, it's that one, go.
So people got impatient with each other.
That definitely happened.
People wanted different things to be decided upon or done, or done in a different order.
Why are you doing that?
I'm really annoyed at you.
That's not the right way to do it, and so on and so forth.
But that is really rich, right?
That is the practice.
We have this really rich, complex moment of trying to figure out how we meet this moment.
A couple of people are a little bit at loggerheads here.
Is it about my own exploration and seeing my own reactivity and doing my own work and letting it go?
Is that probably always part of it?
Is it about some sort of organizational change or improvement?
We need a better process for deciding these things.
We need a more clear agreement about when so-and-so consults with such-and-so.
And we need a way to test it out and then decide together.
And of course, as the six, eight, nine, ten months of construction dragged on, it gets harder and harder to slow it down.
Patience is rich, right?
Where is there room for improvement, and where is there need to be room for just letting go?
It's really hard to discern which is which in any given moment.
So we experiment.
We take it a little too far this way or that.
We hold back too much or we overdo it.
And thank goodness we're in it together, huh?
Thank goodness we're in this together.
We have this shared commitment to awakening, this shared commitment to kindness, the shared commitment to these six practices.
And if something gets out of wonk, I hope sooner or later we work it out.
Maybe with some little improvement in process, or maybe it was just an oops.
We got through it.
Or you think that was an oops and I don't think it was an oops, and that's where we ended up.
Let's move on.
So patience is a lot.
The third paramita I want to talk about is the paramita of energy, virya paramita.
We needed a lot of energy to do this.
Norman Fischer's book on the precepts calls this one enthusiastic energy.
I think that's true.
We had a lot of enthusiasm.
We kept going.
Reb Anderson, another teacher in our lineage, calls it heroic effort.
I don't really use the word hero usually, so I've been enjoying this.
Reb's book is full of it.
He calls these the heroic practices, and this one's heroic effort.
It's nice.
We're kind of like little heroes in our own drama, aren't we?
Like, yes, you're my hero.
Thank you for painting that.
We had to dig deep sometimes into our energy reserves to keep going, work party after work party after work party, and suddenly there's five more emails about another work party.
We had to learn when to take breaks, individually and collectively.
We had to learn how to pace ourselves.
There were times a few of us pushed it too hard and we suffered.
That's how it goes.
We tried to be kind to each other when somebody went a little bit off the rails, because you could see their energy just hit bottom.
And again, I think with generosity and the energy and the patience, it's all of a piece.
And again, that sense of greater purpose.
Like, I'm tired of this now.
I wish it was further along.
It's got to annoy it a little, but it was so-and-so.
But you know what?
I'm going back.
I'm going back.
We need this temple.
The world needs this temple.
This isn't just a thing.
It's something bigger than that.
And here we are, this temple for Northwest Washington.
This temple is actually kind of strengthening the loose tapestry of North American Zen centers.
Many of my colleagues in these other Zen centers, our colleagues, are very excited for us.
We'll see a couple of them on Saturday night.
So that did help our energy.

And virya paramita, again, is the sense of not my energy, but the energy, the collective energy, the energy of the universe, if you will, the energy that I can't even fully understand, but I can be a channel for and a conduit of and expression of as best I can.
All this works better when our minds are more stable.
The little bits of trouble that can happen, I've been mentioning a little bit, come when our minds are unstable, are destabilized.
So one more paramita I want to talk about is concentration, jhana paramita.
That's stabilizing the mind, having a stable mind.
It's interesting that the word jhana, translated here as concentration, is the exact same word as the Chinese character chan, which became the Japanese pronunciation of that character, zen.
So this is the zen paramita, the concentration paramita.
It doesn't just mean meditation, although obviously meditation is a huge causal factor to support our steadiness of concentration.
But it's talking a little bit about attention and mind.
We know that attention can be focused or distracted, right?
Focused or distracted.
But our conventional talk about attention, what we were told in school, which wasn't much besides "pay attention," was our entire instruction on how to manage our attention.
Somebody yelling at us, pay attention, which leads to a certain kind of way of being.
What's interesting about that kind of pay attention, that really narrow, task-focused attention, is that it is stable.
When you're focused on your thing, your mind is stable.
But what our practices help us learn is that there's another kind of stable attention that's not narrow.
It's broad.
It's open.
That's what this paramita is about: a broad, open, stable attention.
Responsive, not as easily ruffled.
It's not rigid.
It has some flow and some give to it.
It's like an equanimity practice.
That kind of attention steadies the mind.
That kind of awareness, that kind of concentration, steadies the mind.
Then it's more possible to be present through a long committee meeting or a long work day, or when 17,000 emails hit your inbox and you wonder, okay, how do I meet this now?
And if I can meet it in that way, a little more stable, it's supportive of energy, patience, generosity, all of them.
They're all totally interconnected in these ways.

So those are four of the six that I think are so obviously in the walls, in the floor: generosity, patience, energy, and concentration, or stability might be a better word for that one, stability of mind.
But the other two are always interwoven as well, so let me mention those briefly.
The second of the six, which I skipped over, is shila paramita, and this is ethics.
It's attention to our behavior throughout our lives, and it's expressed in our practice with the Bodhisattva precepts, this list of guidelines that many of us have made formal commitments to.
Not that we don't forget a few of them from time to time, but then we recommit.
Recommit.
And yes, it's ethical to be generous, and to be patient, to have good energy.
When we aren't ethical, when we take shortcuts or are not fully honest or subvert something or, in our confusion, cause some little bit of harm, then we're diminishing all these great qualities.
These great qualities can't flow and work nearly as well.
So how we actually live and how we hold ourselves, our bearing, our comportment, is really integral.
It's not just being a good person.
It's the expression of the vehicle through which all these can flow more fully.
So that's ethics, shila paramita.
And then the very last one, number six on the list, is wisdom, prajnaparamita.
We're super big fans of this.
It's in our liturgy.
We just chanted it a couple of times there in the service.
Actually, we chanted a whole text that was all about it, didn't we, the Heart Sutra, except we did it in Sino-Japanese, so maybe you didn't recognize it.
This is the wisdom that sees the deeper ground.
This is the wisdom that isn't only dazzled by the surfaces and by our opinions and by what we tend to think out of habit.
This is the wisdom that helps us go deep and see the interconnectedness of everything.
The wisdom of really feeling the natural flow of reality.
It may seem like we worked really hard to build this temple, which is true, but the temple also just unfolded in the way it needed to.
So this is the wisdom of our temple-building paramita practice.

Thanks.

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** That's nice.
In the end, all is well.
So if all is well, it's not the end.
Expectations.
Isn't that interesting?
I have so much suffering.
And we had so many expectations about this building.
Huge list.
This is the wonderful thing, that it's just so much better.
Better than our expectations.

I just feel building is a community activity.
We're all tight and worried about our expectations, and that's actually limiting.
We're not imagining big enough.
We're not going big enough.
